Nations are turning to the defense industry to fill diminished inventories, but in the United States, governmental financial constraints make this an impossible task. Reduced defense funding hampers or prevents stockpile revitalization.

The current constraints on defense funding are the results of policy decisions. For one, wartime supplemental funding in the United States is not available for indirect or proxy conflicts, and unfortunately, traditional deterrence, a flawed premise for preventing direct conflict, has resulted in the ill-conceived justification for diverting funds from defense to social endeavors.

When deterrence fails, industry will be asked to respond. Thus, the underlying pinnacle but least-recognized instrument of deterrence is the strength of a nation’s economy and production capability. Industrial strength as a backstop to deterrence makes negotiations, sanctions and military status more likely to be effective.

If international negotiations are to be sincere, sanctions to be penetrating and military prowess to be acknowledged, then we must focus on domestic industrial capability. The U.S. supply chain is now spread out farther overseas than in previous years, which hastens the decline in industrial capability and production readiness.

The United States as a dominant economic power is slipping to the rise of China. U.S. competitiveness has been ranked as ninth globally. This position has been consistent over the years, but China’s competitiveness, according to multiple sources — the World Bank, etc. — is gaining, closer to 25 percent now. Its annual percentage increase in industrial production was 6.1 percent versus the United States’ 2.3 percent, according to the CIA World Factbook. As far back as 2015, the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development highlighted China exceeding the United States in global manufacturing. Manufacturing in the United States is approximately 11 percent of the nation’s GDP, and the growth rate is 2.2 percent, which is below the world average of 2.9 percent, according to data from the National Institute of Standards and Technology.
The shuffle between rising and falling economic powers is a source of potential conflict because previous deterrence power by one is no longer a concern of the rising economic nation.

An Oct. 1, 2023, article by Ling Chen and Miles Evers, titled, “Wars Without Gun Smoke,” describes economic statecraft as it relates to global widening of the supply chain. Trade restrictions are an effort to slow the rise of competitive nations economically and in turn preserve U.S. deterrence capabilities for actions contrary to U.S. national security.

Strengthening U.S. manufacturing is only possible by increasing demand for products, and demand is a function of attractiveness, utility and innovation. In the last several decades, U.S. policymakers have looked more to the commercial sector to advance technology that can be applied toward defense requirements.

Although commercial innovation cannot be overlooked, it should not be viewed as an offset to defense research and development, which by its nature is specifically targeted to thwart potential threats to national security.

In the 1970s — with the Cold War a major concern — the defense industry led the way in the pursuit of state-of-the-art technology, for example, creating GPS and the internet. As time passed and the Cold War ended, the government shifted its attention to reaping benefits from the commercial sector’s exploration and advances in technology.

The use of defense technology applied dually in the commercial sector and in defense has now flip-flopped to where commercial products, such as unmanned aerial vehicles, cybersecurity technology and artificial intelligence are now applied to defense.

The defense industry has been relegated to a fast-follower position. This shift has been the justification for drawing down government-sponsored defense industry research and development. Science and innovation funding was approximately 4 percent of the 2022 defense budget — a number insufficient to sustain even small companies focused on advancing promising technology and likewise below a threshold allowing larger firms to continue specific targeted development, according to a McKinsey & Company Nov. 4, 2022, article authored by Eric Chewning, Will Gangware, Jess Harrington and Dale Swartz.
The shift toward relying on the commercial sector for innovation has also lessened dependence on U.S. technology worldwide and fostered a desire or preference for overseas-manufactured products.

U.S. strength in advanced technology development and manufacturing has dropped from its peak position. To halt this decline and regain our prominence, governmental policies must encourage industry by supplying favorable tax credits, an improved regulatory environment and reduced energy costs.

In cross-table international discussions of commercial and defense issues, the United States has been relegated to a peer level of importance instead of remaining the leader. The administration seeks to avoid direct military involvement; therefore, emphasis must be placed on economic fortitude across all manufacturing sectors, with special consideration of responsiveness in times of conflict.

The recipient of increased funding should be the defense industry because of its history of tackling technical challenges, innovating solutions and creating a supply chain that is predominantly domestic for national security reasons. Defense contractors are less sensitive to pressure from investors who are seeking shorter development cycles, and they have extensive experience solving complex engineering challenges.

The defense establishment, both governmental and industrial players, have worked together for decades developing state-of-the-art technology, retiring risk, adjusting milestones and fostering technical expertise within the workforce.
With the introduction of each new product, the domestic and international marketplace will respond positively, increasing demand and strengthening U.S. industrial strength and deterrence power.
Domestic economic health is a critical component of deterrence.
